'''Nicholas A. Kotov''' (born August 29, 1965, in [[Moscow]], [[USSR]]) is the [[Irving Langmuir]] Distinguished University Professor of Chemical Sciences and Engineering and the Joseph B. and Florence V. Cejka Professor of Engineering at the [[University of Michigan]] in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], United States.<ref>{{cite web
|title=Nicholas A. Kotov Joseph B. and Florence V. Cejka Professor of Chemical Engineering
|url=https://che.engin.umich.edu/people/kotov-nicholas/
|website=Michigan Engineering
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref> He is the Director of the National Science Foundation Science and Technology Center for Complex Particle Systems (COMPASS), developing graph-based methods for design of materials essential for sustainability..<ref>{{cite web
|title=Center for Complex Particle Systems (COMPASS),
|url=https://compass.engin.umich.edu/
|website=University of Michigan
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref> 

Kotov is known for pioneering studies on nanoparticle self-organization, biomimetic materials, and chiral nanostructures. Kotov demonstrated that structurally imperfect inorganic nanoparticles can self-assemble into complex hierarchical structures resembling biological assemblies and materials.<ref>{{cite news
|title=ACS Award in Colloid Chemistry: Nicholas A. Kotov
|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i1/ACS-Award-Colloid-Chemistry-NicholasKotov.html
|publisher=Chemical & Engineering News
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|title=Dr. Nicholas A. Kotov
|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/bio/dr-nicholas-kotov
|website=AIChE.org
|date=12 October 2020
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|last=Jiang
|first=Wenfeng
|title=Emergence of complexity in hierarchically organized chiral particles
|journal=Science
|year=2020
|volume=368
|issue=6491
|pages=642–648
|doi=10.1126/science.aaz7949
|pmid=32273399
|hdl=10447/626100
|hdl-access=free
}}</ref> He established self-organization as an intrinsic characteristic of nanoscale systems, which contributed to the development of biomimetic composites combining mechanical, optical, and functional properties that are rarely achieved simultaneously in conventional materials.<ref>{{cite web
|title=RSC Award Lecture at Hull University
|url=https://www.rsc.org/events/detail/26480/award-lecture-at-hull-university
|website=RSC.org
|date=20 May 2016
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref> These composite biomimetic materials are exemplified by nacre-like composites from clay and graphene oxide,<ref>{{cite news
|title=U-M research: Making Plastic as Strong as Steel
|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/making-plastic-as-strong/
|publisher=Scientific American
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|last=Kotov
|first=Nicholas A.
|title=Ultrathin graphite oxide-polyelectrolyte composites prepared by self-assembly: Transition between conductive and non-conductive states
|journal=Advanced Materials
|year=1996
|volume=8
|issue=8
|pages=637–641
|doi=10.1002/adma.19960080806
}}</ref> and cartilage-like membranes from cellulose nanofibrils and aramid nanofibers.<ref>{{cite news
|title=Membrane inspired by bone and cartilage efficiently produces electricity from saltwater
|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/12/191218153539.htm
|publisher=ScienceDaily
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|title=Inspired by the Tissues of Living Organisms, Researchers Take One Step Closer to Harvesting "Blue Energy"
|url=https://e360.yale.edu/digest/inspired-by-the-tissues-of-living-organisms-researchers-take-one-step-closer-to-harvesting-blue-energy
|publisher=Yale Environment 360
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref> Kotov is also known for pioneering chiral nanostructures exhibiting exceptionally strong optical activity.<ref>{{cite journal
|last=Chen
|first=Wei
|title=Nanoparticle Superstructures Made by Polymerase Chain Reaction: Collective Interactions of Nanoparticles and a New Principle for Chiral Materials
|journal=Nano Letters
|year=2009
|volume=9
|issue=5
|pages=2153–2159
|doi=10.1021/nl900726s
|pmid=19320495
}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|title=UMich researcher receives $10 million grant for nanoparticle design research
|url=https://www.michigandaily.com/news/research/umich-researcher-nicholas-kotov-receives-10-million-grant-for-nanoparticle-design-research/
|publisher=The Michigan Daily
|access-date=26 February 2026
}}</ref> 

Materials he developed have enabled sustainable energy devices, green catalysis, and aramid recycling. The chiral plasmonic nanoparticles are being tested for early detection of cancer.<ref>{{cite web
|title=Faster, more sensitive lung cancer detection from a blood draw

}}</ref><ref>{{cite web

}}</ref>

==Work==
Kotov's research is focused on the development of biomimetic nanocomposites, the [[self-assembly]] of [[nanoparticle]]s,<ref name="tang">{{cite journal|author1=Zhiyong Tang|author2=Nicholas A. Decher|author2=J. D. Hong|author3=J. Schmitt|year=1992|title=Buildup of ultrathin multilayer films by a self-assembly process: III. Consecutively alternating adsorption of anionic and cationic polyelectrolytes on charged surfaces|journal=Thin Solid Films|volume=210/211|page=831|bibcode=1992TSF...210..831D|doi=10.1016/0040-6090(92)90417-A}}</ref> Kotov prepared a wide spectrum of nacre-like nanocomposites including those from clay<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kotov|first1=N. A.|last2=Magonov|first2=S.|last3=Tropsha|first3=E.|date=March 1998|title=Layer-by-Layer Self-Assembly of Alumosilicate−Polyelectrolyte Composites: Mechanism of Deposition, Crack Resistance, and A.|last2=Dékány|first2=Imre|last3=Fendler|first3=Janos H.|date=August 1996|title=Ultrathin graphite oxide-polyelectrolyte composites prepared by self-assembly: Transition between conductive and non-conductive states|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/adma.19960080806|journal=Advanced Materials|language=en|volume=8|issue=8|pages=637–641|doi=10.1002/adma.19960080806|bibcode=1996AdM.....8..637K |url-access=subscription}}</ref> He showed that clay-based biomimetic composites can attain mechanical properties comparable to some grades of steel while retaining transparency.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Podsiadlo|first1=Paul|last2=Kaushik|first2=Amit K.|last3=Arruda|author3-link= Ellen Arruda|first3=Ellen M.|last4=Waas|first4=Anthony M.|last5=Shim|first5=Bong Sup|last6=Xu|first6=Jiadi|last7=Nandivada|first7=Himabindu|last8=Pumplin|first8=Benjamin G.|last9=Lahann|first9=Joerg|date=2007-10-05|title=Ultrastrong and Stiff Layered Polymer Nanocomposites|journal=Science|language=en|volume=318|issue=5847|pages=80–83|doi=10.1126/science.1143176|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17916728|bibcode=2007Sci...318...80P|s2cid=22559961}}</ref> This discovery spurred the development of new methods for the mass-production of nacre-like materials from a large variety of inorganic nanosheets.<ref>{{Cite |title=Professor Nicholas Kotov

}}</ref>

Kotov extended the concept of [[Biomimetics|biomimetic]] nanostructures to inorganic [[nanoparticle]]s. He established that, similarly to many proteins and other biomolecules, nanoparticles can self-organize into chains,<ref name="tang" /> sheets,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Zhiyong Tang|author2=Zhenli Zhang|author3=Ying Wang|author4=Sharon C. Glotzer|author5=Nicholas A. Kotov|s2cid=22492581|doi-access=free}}</ref> and nanohelices,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhou|first1=Yunlong|last2=Marson|first2=Ryan L.|last3=van Anders|first3=Greg|last4=Zhu|first4=Jian|last5=Ma|first5=Guanxiang|last6=Ercius|first6=Peter|last7=Sun|first7=Kai|last8=Yeom|first8=Bongjun|last9=Glotzer|first9=Sharon C.|date=2016-03-22|title=Biomimetic Hierarchical Assembly of Helical Supraparticles from Chiral Nanoparticles|journal=ACS Nano|volume=10|issue=3|pages=3248–3256|doi=10.1021/acsnano.5b05983|pmid=26900920|bibcode=2016ACSNa..10.3248Z |osti=1440921|s2cid=30561840 |issn=1936-0851|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9r7892xp }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Feng|first1=Wenchun|last2=Kim|first2=Ji-Young|last3=Wang|first3=Xinzhi|last4=Calcaterra|first4=Heather A.|last5=Qu|first5=Zhibei|last6=Meshi|first6=Louisa|last7=Kotov|first7=Nicholas A.|date=2017-03-01|title=Assembly of mesoscale helices with near-unity enantiomeric excess and light-matter interactions for chiral semiconductors|journal=Science Advances|language=en|volume=3|issue=3|article-number=e1601159|doi=10.1126/sciadv.1601159|pmid=28275728|pmc=5332156|bibcode=2017SciA....3E1159F |issn=2375-2548}}</ref> and spherical supraparticles replicating viral capsids.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xia|first1=Yunsheng|last2=Nguyen|first2=Trung Dac|last3=Yang|first3=Ming|last4=Lee|first4=Byeongdu|last5=Santos|first5=Aaron|last6=Podsiadlo|first6=Paul|last7=Tang|first7=Zhiyong|last8=Glotzer|first8=Sharon C.|last9=Kotov|first9=Nicholas A.|date=2011-08-21|title=Self-assembly of self-limiting monodisperse supraparticles from polydisperse nanoparticles|journal=Nature Nanotechnology|language=en|volume=6|issue=9|pages=580–587|doi=10.1038/nnano.2011.121|pmid=21857686|bibcode=2011NatNa...6..580X |issn=1748-3395}}</ref>

Kotov's work established that the biomimetic self-assembly behavior of nanoparticles originates from interparticle interactions at the nanoscale,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Batista|first1=Carlos A. Silvera|last2=Larson|first2=Ronald G.|last3=Kotov|first3=Nicholas A.|date=2015-10-09|title=Nonadditivity of nanoparticle interactions|journal=Science|language=en|volume=350|issue=6257|article-number=1242477|doi=10.1126/science.1242477|issn=0036-8075|pmid=26450215|doi-access=free}}</ref> in which chirality also plays a prominent role.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ma|first1=Wei|last2=Xu|first2=Liguang|last3=de Moura|first3=André F.|last4=Wu|first4=Xiaoling|last5=Kuang|first5=Hua|last6=Xu|first6=Chuanlai|last7=Kotov|first7=Nicholas A.|date=2017-06-28|title=Chiral Inorganic Nanostructures|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=117|issue=12|pages=8041–8093|doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.6b00755|pmid=28426196|issn=0009-2665}}</ref> His studies on the self-assembly of chiral nanostructures have led to the development of nanoparticle assemblies with complexity exceeding those found in biological organisms.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Wenfeng|last2=Qu|first2=Zhi-bei|last3=Kumar|first3=Prashant|last4=Vecchio|first4=Drew|last5=Wang|first5=Yuefei|last6=Ma|first6=Yu|last7=Bahng|first7=Joong Hwan|last8=Bernardino|first8=Kalil|last9=Gomes|first9=Weverson R.|last10=Colombari|first10=Felippe M.|last11=Lozada-Blanco|first11=Asdrubal|date=2020-05-08|title=Emergence of complexity in hierarchically organized chiral particles|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaz7949|journal=Science|language=en|volume=368|issue=6491|pages=642–648|doi=10.1126/science.aaz7949|pmid=32273399 |bibcode=2020Sci...368..642J |s2cid=215726726 |issn=0036-8075|hdl=10447/626100|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Education and research career==

===Education and early career===
Kotov received his MS (1987) and [[PhD]] (1990) degrees in [[chemistry]] from [[Moscow State University]], where his research concerned liquid-liquid interfaces imitating cell membranes for [[solar power|solar energy conversion]]. After graduation, he took up a postdoctoral position in the research group of Prof. Janos Fendler in the Department of Chemistry at [[Syracuse University]] in [[New York (state)|New York]] state working on nanoparticle synthesis and assembly at interfaces.

===Independent research career===
Kotov took up a position as assistant professor of chemistry at the [[Oklahoma State University–Stillwater|Oklahoma State University]] in [[Stillwater, Oklahoma]] in 1996, gaining promotion to associate professor in 2001. In 2003 he moved to the [[University of Michigan]] where he is now the Irving Langmuir Distinguished Professor of Chemical Sciences and Engineering.

==Personal life==
Kotov married chemist Elvira Stesikova, PhD, in 1991. They have two daughters, Sophia and Nicole.
